correctness.rationale: The geodesic side supporting-line relation, disjoint forbidden arcs, and polar area Jacobian prove the exact radial density. A verified antiderivative gives the piecewise CDF and normalization; local Taylor expansions give the sharp 3/2 transition and fixed-n cusp tail. Taking t=log n+s in the explicit formula yields a continuous normalized limiting CDF, hence convergence in distribution. The included standalone checker passed independent density quadrature, area-point Monte Carlo, transition tests and n=10000 convergence tests.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The fixed-polygon nearest-side theorem permits arbitrary ideal polygons but measures a different variable; its broader polygon class does not imply this radial law. The random cyclic-polygon theorem studies area of a random hull with radius of order logarithmic in sample size; despite the log scale it does not entail the centered radial distribution of deterministic ideal polygons.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: A Liouville-random geodesic chord can traverse the ideal polygon in infinitely many ways, while the present experiment samples one point by finite hyperbolic area. Nearest-side clearance has bounded support (the inradius) but center distance is unbounded. A random ideal-triangle incenter under random boundary vertices and random finite-circle polygon area have different sample spaces and statistics. The exact finite-n radial CDF and the many-side law cannot be recovered as corollaries of these inspected statements.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The natural equivalent event is area of the intersection of the polygon with a centered hyperbolic disk, or the distribution of the radius of an area-uniform interior point. Xu instead calculates Liouville-random geodesic chord lengths; the boundary-distance paper calculates nearest-side clearance. Neither supplies the centered-disk intersection area, even by a change of marginal variables.

value.rationale: Regular ideal polygons are canonical noncompact finite-area domains; the distribution of center-distance from an area-uniform point quantifies how their area escapes down ideal cusps. The exact incircle angular-loss transition, explicit uncoupled many-side limit and its two different exponential tails give substantive shape information not reducible to a single moment or routine fixed-n disk calculation. The logarithmic shift and limiting incircle mass 2/pi are natural geometric diagnostics.
